message.content:
**Signatures on the U.S. Declaration of Independence**

When the Continental Congress adopted the text on **July 2, 1776**, it sent copies to each colony so they could approve them locally.  
On **August 2–5, 1776**, delegates gathered at the Pennsylvania State House (now Independence Hall) in Philadelphia to sign the official copy that would become part of the National Archives.  

There were **56 signers**—one representative from each of the thirteen colonies who had ratified independence. Below is the complete roster, grouped by state:

| Colony | Signer(s) |
|--------|-----------|
| **Delaware** | Samuel Chase, William Paca |
| **Pennsylvania** | John Dickinson, Joseph Hewes, James Smith |
| **New Jersey** | Francis Hopkinson, Richard Stockton |
| **Georgia** | Button Gwinnett, Lyman Hall |
| **Connecticut** | Abraham Baldwin, Oliver Wolcott |
| **Massachusetts** | John Adams, Paul Revere, John Hancock, Charles Lee, Samuel Whitman |
| **Maryland** | Daniel Carroll, Edward Lloyd |
| **South Carolina** | Henry Laurens, Arthur Middleton |
| **North Carolina** | Josiah Martin, William Hooper |
| **Virginia** | Patrick Henry, Edmund Randolph, George Wythe |
| **Rhode Island** | Stephen Hopkins, William Ellery |
| **New Hampshire** | Matthew Thornton, Jeremiah Moulton |
| **Tennessee** *(then part of North Carolina)* | — (no separate signer – represented by NC delegates) |

> *Note:* Some states had more than one delegate due to multiple representatives being elected before the vote. For example, Delaware’s two signers came from its two congressional seats.

### Key Points About Signing

1. **George Washington** attended the session as commander‑in‑chief of the Continental Army but did **not** sign the declaration because his signature appeared on the “Provisional Constitution” instead. He later became the first President of the United States.

2. **Thomas Jefferson** drafted the initial version of the Declaration while serving as Secretary of State under President George Washington. Though he never physically signed the printed copy presented to the Congress, his handwriting appears on the draft manuscript preserved today.

3. **Benjamin Franklin** was among the most senior members of the committee that prepared the final wording. His signature is famously written in a single line across the bottom of the parchment.

4. Many signers’ names have survived only through their inked marks on the parchment. In several cases, the original signatures were lost or damaged over time, leading historians to rely on photographs taken in the early 19th century.

5. The act of signing itself carried political weight: once a colonist affixed his seal, he publicly committed himself—and his community—to the cause of independence, risking imprisonment if British forces regained control.

---

#### Quick Reference List (Alphabetical)

```
Abraham Baldwin          - Connecticut
Samuel Chase              - Delaware
John Dickinson            - Pennsylvania
Joseph Hewes              - Pennsylvania
James Smith               - Pennsylvania
Francis Hopkinson         - New Jersey
Richard Stockton          - New Jersey
Button Gwinnett           - Georgia
Lyman Hall                - Georgia
Oliver Wolcott            - Connecticut
Paul Revere               - Massachusetts
Charles Lee               - Massachusetts
Samuel Whitman            - Massachusetts
Daniel Carroll            - Maryland
Edward Lloyd              - Maryland
Henry Laurens             - South Carolina
Arthur Middleton          - South Carolina
Josiah Martin             - North Carolina
William Hooper             - North Carolina
Patrick Henry             - Virginia
Edmund Randolph           - Virginia
George Wythe              - Virginia
Stephen Hopkins           - Rhode Island
William Ellery            - Rhode Island
Matthew Thornton          - New Hampshire
Jeremiah Moulton          - New Hampshire
Robert R. Livingston      - New York (though NY didn’t send a delegation until after the adoption)
```

*(For brevity, this list omits duplicate entries where a colony had multiple signers.)*

These individuals collectively forged the foundational legal document that declared the Thirteen Colonies independent from Great Britain. Their signatures remain emblematic symbols of American liberty and civic duty.
